5.label: Foundations first
5.text: Organisations that keep pursuing growth without repairing their foundations eventually exhaust themselves. Sustainable strategy restores the core capabilities and values that support long-term performance.

6.label: Strategy becomes structure
6.text: A vision remains fragile when responsibilities are unclear, resources are poorly managed and essential activities depend on a few individuals. Strong strategy asks what capabilities, roles, resources and operating rhythms will make the achievement possible. Many organisations fail because the supporting system was never designed.

6.label: G · Governance
6.text: Build governance structures with the power to prevent decisions that will harm the organisation. A structure that can only register objections leaves the harm in place.

7.label: Beyond extraordinary effort
7.text: An organisation cannot rely indefinitely on extraordinary effort. Sustainable results need structures that protect what has been achieved, with the right behaviours embedded in responsibilities and systems.

9.label: R · Resource the people who carry it
9.text: Organisations that run their best people to exhaustion before the work is done lose their most valuable asset at the moment of greatest need. Build the conditions, rhythms and support that let people finish the work at full capacity.

9.label: Communication and capability
9.text: Knowledge of standards does not guarantee behaviour. Implementation needs capability, reinforcement and environmental support alongside communication.

13.label: S · Systems
13.text: Strategic drift sets in when platforms, policies, structures or projects become ends in themselves. Ask repeatedly whether institutional assets still produce the intended value.

13.label: R · Unsustainable workloads
13.text: Organisations that give people no margin to renew and recover produce people who eventually cannot run at all. The rhythm of renewal is part of the design of sustainable excellence.

13.label: R · Capacity to deploy
13.text: Organisations underestimate available resource when they have not invested in the capacity to deploy it: the people, processes and structures that turn opportunity into output. Ask what the organisation is prepared to receive and deploy, alongside what it has.

13.label: G · Selective accountability
13.text: Structures that let certain roles accumulate disproportionate influence without a reset mechanism eventually produce internal inequality. Review concentrations of resource, influence and opportunity periodically.

14.label: Naming unsustainable practice
14.text: A culture that cannot name its unsustainable practices before they produce a breakdown keeps managing consequences and leaves the causes untouched. Create room for an outside voice that can name what insiders are too close to see.

14.label: Honest signals
14.text: Organisations become more intelligent when difficult information is incorporated into decisions. Honest signals can improve direction. Use this with “Friction as organisational intelligence”.

14.label: Values misalignment
14.text: When espoused values and rewarded behaviours diverge, people calibrate to the real signal and discount the stated one. The work is closing the distance between declaration and practice.

20.label: Culture is formed deliberately
20.text: People cannot live by standards they have never understood. Repeated teaching creates a common language through which behaviour can be interpreted and corrected, and culture becomes credible when declared beliefs are visible in everyday behaviour.

21.label: Values before commercial pressure
21.text: Organisations that make commercial success the primary culture signal produce cultures where ethical shortcuts become routine whenever they pay. Value clarity must come before commercial pressure.

22.label: Step 1 · Define the behaviour
22.text: Many cultural change initiatives fail because they operate at the level of slogans and posters. Translate one value into a specific operational instruction: what the team does, in what circumstance, by default, when the leader is absent.

22.label: Step 3 · Write the norm statement
22.text: When new staff ask “what should I actually do here?”, a healthy culture gives concrete, immediate answers. Take one value, write down the single specific action that proves it, and say it out loud to the team.

23.label: Test 1 · The New Employee Test
23.text: Audit the culture by asking whether a stranger watching the team for a week could infer the stated values from what people actually do. Knowledge that changes no behaviour is decoration.

23.label: Test 2 · The Pressure Test
23.text: Culture becomes most visible when normal conditions disappear. A culture may claim empowerment until something goes wrong and every decision is pulled upward, or claim openness until someone challenges a senior leader.

23.label: Test 3 · The Mirror Test
23.text: Reforms announced for the rest of the organisation will not hold until the compromised practice inside the leader’s own team is dismantled. Identify one celebrated habit in your team that contradicts a value you espouse, and dismantle it before asking anyone else to change.

24.label: Beyond the leader’s presence
24.text: Whatever the culture does because the leader is watching will stop when the leader is absent. Convert leader-dependent behaviours into structurally embedded ones through systems, rituals and named commitments.

24.label: Hosting the value
24.text: New cultural commitments are often launched with ceremony and then passed from team to team because no one does the work of hosting them. Name the function or team that will carry each norm.

25.label: A complete response
25.text: Organisations that discover a fundamental misalignment between stated values and actual practice face a choice: respond completely, or address only what is comfortable. The part left untouched is the part that resurfaces.
